questions.q: Why should a benchmark report latency percentiles (p50, p90, p99) instead of just the average?
options: An average can look identical whether most requests are fast with a few catastrophic outliers, or everything is uniformly mediocre — those need different fixes
Percentiles eliminate the need to measure throughput
Averages are not mathematically valid for latency data
Percentiles are easier to calculate than averages
questions.explain: A single average hides the shape of the distribution. Two very different situations — rare severe outliers versus uniformly mediocre performance — can produce the same average but require completely different remedies.

questions.q: Why is testing at a single fixed concurrency level insufficient for benchmarking a serving stack?
options: Fixed concurrency tests are always faster to run
Fixed concurrency only works for CPU-based services
It can miss the point where the system's behavior changes significantly as load increases, which a concurrency ramp (e.g., 1, 10, 50, 200) is designed to find
Concurrency has no effect on inference performance
questions.explain: Behavior under load often changes nonlinearly — queuing effects, batching limits, and contention can appear only past a certain concurrency. A ramp finds where that happens; a single fixed level can miss it entirely.

questions.q: What problem does skipping a warm-up pass create in a benchmark?
options: It makes the benchmark run faster with more accurate results
Warm-up passes are only relevant for CPU-only workloads
It has no measurable effect on results
One-time startup costs, like CUDA kernel compilation or cache population, can skew the earliest measurements away from steady-state performance
questions.explain: The first few requests often pay one-time initialization costs that don't represent ongoing, steady-state performance, so discarding them or warming up first gives a more representative result.

questions.q: What does it mean for 'the client to become the bottleneck' during a benchmark?
options: The client and server are always perfectly balanced
This only happens when testing with a single request
The load-generating machine itself runs out of CPU, network bandwidth, or connections, so the test actually measures the client's limits rather than the server's
The server being tested is always the only possible bottleneck
questions.explain: If the load generator can't actually produce or receive traffic fast enough, the measured results reflect the client's limitations, not the real capacity of the serving stack under test.

questions.q: Why does a benchmark need realistic prompt and output length distributions rather than all-short, uniform test inputs?
options: A workload of all-short prompts and outputs under-represents the cost and latency of longer requests that appear in real production traffic
Uniform short prompts always produce the most accurate percentiles
Prompt length has no effect on inference cost or latency
Realistic prompt lengths are only relevant for image models
questions.explain: Since prefill and decode cost scale with token counts, a benchmark using only short, uniform prompts will systematically understate the latency and cost behavior of the long-context or long-generation requests production traffic actually contains.
